notes: Complex confiscation appeal on gifted property; conviction leave refused out of time; order reduced to agreed £52,250.

enrichment.short_title: Greet: confiscation order varied after Pembroke Road gift to associate
key_facts: Michael Greet, a Bristol solicitor, was convicted in December 2001 of theft of about £487,000 from client accounts, making a false trust deed, and failing to keep proper accounting records as a bankrupt.

In November 2003 the trial judge made a confiscation order for £160,000 with 18 months imprisonment in default, treating a July 1997 transfer of Pembroke Road to Ms Thompson as a tainted gift represented in Chantry Road.
Greet applied very late for leave to appeal against conviction based on fresh evidence about his bookkeeper's gambling, but the court refused extension of time and leave.
On the confiscation appeal the court held the gift should be taken into account and substituted an order for £52,250 with nine months in default.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction and appeal with leave against a confiscation order under the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal against conviction refused; confiscation appeal allowed in part by quashing the £160,000 order and substituting £52,250 with imprisonment in default reduced to nine months.
enrichment.ratio: A transfer of property to a closely connected associate funded from office accounts and linked to the defendant's offending may be treated as a gift caught by the confiscation legislation; section 74(10) discretion is an all-or-nothing decision on the gift as a whole, while section 71(1) permits a tailored confiscation figure.
legal_issues: Whether the Pembroke Road transfer was a gift made by the defendant for section 74 purposes
Whether consideration or a trustee compromise defeated gift status
How gifted equity rolled into Chantry Road should be valued under section 74(8)
Whether fresh evidence justified late leave to appeal against conviction
linked_authorities: R v Lee [1996] QB 1
R v Norris [2001] 1 WLR 1388
R v A [2003] EWCA Crim 2849

notes: Foundational forced-marriage inherent jurisdiction judgment for an adult; postscript records swift consular resolution.

enrichment.short_title: Re SK: High Court inherent jurisdiction over threatened forced marriage of adult
key_facts: SK, a young adult British citizen habitually resident in England, was believed to be in Bangladesh facing forced marriage or restraint by relatives.
The Foreign Office Community Liaison Unit instructed solicitors to bring ex parte proceedings without notice to SK or her family.
Singer J held the High Court's inherent jurisdiction could extend to adults deprived of effective autonomy, analogous to wardship and declaratory relief in medical cases.

Orders included marriage injunctions, protection from harassment, bench orders for relatives' attendance, and consular interview in Dhaka; proceedings were later discontinued after SK returned and said intervention was unnecessary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Ex parte originating summons on the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court in forced marriage proceedings reserved to Singer J.
enrichment.outcome: The court exercised jurisdiction and made protective orders; after consular interview SK returned to England and the proceedings were discontinued, but the judgment clarified availability of relief for adults.
enrichment.ratio: Where an emancipated adult may be unable to exercise free will because of duress or forced marriage, the High Court may use its inherent jurisdiction to investigate circumstances abroad and make injunctions and directions even though an adult cannot be made a ward of court.
legal_issues: Whether the courts of England and Wales have jurisdiction over a British adult abroad facing forced marriage
How inherent jurisdiction compares with wardship for minors
What protective orders are proportionate on indirect ex parte evidence
Whether forced marriage proceedings should attract public funding
linked_authorities: Re S (Hospital patient: court's jurisdiction) [1996] Fam 1
A v A Health Authority [2002] EWHC 18 (Fam/Admin)
P v R (Forced Marriage: Annulment) [2003] 1 FLR 661

confidence.notes: Novel but concise judgment with clear jurisdictional reasoning and postscript outcome.

notes: Operation Care historic abuse appeal; JA convictions quashed after post-trial retraction, sentence cut to ten years.

enrichment.short_title: Sutton: partial unsafe conviction appeal in Operation Care children's home case
key_facts: Richard Sutton, a care worker, was convicted in 2001 of numerous historic sexual offences against PH, PD, PV and JA at Merseyside children's homes and sentenced to fourteen years.
Grounds included inadequate corroboration and delay warnings, alleged Operation Care compensation priming, and complainant-specific challenges.
The court admitted post-trial compensation applications by PD and PV and evidence that JA had retracted his trial evidence in September 2001.
Convictions relating to JA were held unsafe because he would not attend to support or explain his retraction; other convictions stood and total sentence was reduced to ten years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full Court of Appeal hearing after referral of leave application in a long-delayed historic abuse conviction appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal granted; appeal allowed in part by quashing JA-related convictions and reducing sentence from fourteen to ten years imprisonment; remaining convictions upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Hope of compensation does not of itself make complainant evidence unreliable, but where a key witness retracts trial evidence and refuses to attend court the resulting uncertainty can render related convictions unsafe without affecting other complainants' verdicts.
legal_issues: Adequacy of jury warnings on unsupported complainant evidence and delay
Whether Operation Care non-disclosure about compensation tainted the trial
Admissibility of post-trial compensation claims and JA's retraction
Whether inconsistent PH verdicts demonstrated unsafe conviction
linked_authorities: R v Makanjuola [1995] 2 Cr App Rep 469
R v Williams-Rigby [2003] EWCA Crim 693
R v Durante 56 Cr App R 708

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate reasoning with explicit partial allowance and sentence adjustment.

notes: Costs appeal after exaggerated PI claim; university treated as real winner despite beating Part 36 payment.

enrichment.short_title: Painting v Oxford: costs reversed after exaggerated ladder-fall claim
key_facts: Mrs Painting fell from a ladder at work and claimed about £400,000 after a twenty per cent contributory negligence deduction; liability was admitted.
The University paid £184,442.91 into court in February 2004 but withdrew all but £10,000 after discovering surveillance undermining the severity of her injuries.
The recorder awarded only £25,331.78, finding deliberate exaggeration and recovery by late 2002/early 2003, yet ordered the University to pay all her costs.
The Court of Appeal held the University was the effective winner on exaggeration and that the inadequate Part 36 payment did not outweigh claimant misconduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a county court recorder's costs order following assessment of damages in a personal injury action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; recorder's costs order set aside and replaced with an order that the University pay Mrs Painting's costs to 25 February 2004 and that she pay the University's costs thereafter.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 44.3 a claimant who beats an inadequate Part 36 payment is not automatically entitled to costs where she deliberately exaggerated the claim and the defendant succeeded on the central issue; conduct including failure to negotiate must be weighed in the overall justice of the case.
legal_issues: Interaction of Part 36 success with CPR 44.3 conduct and exaggeration factors
Whether the recorder erred by treating the limited payment-in window as decisive
Who was the real winner where damages were only about six per cent of the claim
Effect of surveillance evidence exposing misleading medical presentation
linked_authorities: Islam v Ali [2003] EWCA Civ 612
Malloy v Shell UK Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 1272
Tanfern v Cameron McDonald [2000] 1 WLR 13

confidence.notes: Focused costs appeal with clear substituted order and detailed CPR analysis.

notes: Major libel appeal upholding Reynolds privilege rejection and presumption of damage in corporate defamation.

enrichment.short_title: Jameel v WSJE: Reynolds privilege and presumption of damage upheld
key_facts: The Wall Street Journal Europe published an article in February 2002 suggesting Saudi officials were monitoring bank accounts with potential terrorist links, understood to refer to Mr Jameel and his Saudi trading company.
A jury found publication defamatory and awarded £30,000 to Mr Jameel and £10,000 to the company; Eady J rejected Reynolds qualified privilege.
The publishers appealed on Reynolds privilege, the presumption of damage, and applications relating to the presumption of falsity.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the privilege and presumption-of-damage appeals and refused permission to appeal on falsity grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against Eady J's rulings in a jury libel trial concerning qualified privilege and presumption of damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals on Reynolds privilege and presumption of damage dismissed; applications for permission to appeal on presumption of falsity refused.
enrichment.ratio: Reynolds privilege requires responsible journalism including fair opportunity to comment and proper regard to privacy and public interest; the common law presumption of damage in corporate libel is compatible with Article 10 and necessary for vindication where financial loss is hard to prove.
legal_issues: What must be pleaded and proved for Reynolds qualified privilege
Whether naming monitored account holders was in the public interest
Whether Article 10 requires proof of special damage by corporate claimants
Whether the presumption of falsity or jury directions infringed Convention rights
linked_authorities: Reynolds v Times Newspapers [2001] 2 AC 127
Derbyshire CC v Times Newspapers [1993] AC 534
McDonalds Corporation v Steel & Morris [1999] All ER (D) 384

confidence.notes: Leading libel appellate judgment with explicit dismissal of multiple grounds.

notes: Attorney General reference; unduly lenient life minimum term for sexually motivated murder increased.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference 130/2004: murder minimum term increased from 14 to 16 years
key_facts: A 19-year-old offender pleaded guilty to murdering Corinne Bailey and attempting to cause grievous bodily harm to Julie Francis in Croydon in August 2003.
The attacks were sexually motivated; Bailey suffered extreme violence with a piece of wood and Francis was throttled after a prostitute encounter.
Astill J imposed custody for life with a fourteen-year minimum term after a twenty-year starting point, giving credit for age and late guilty plea.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient and the Court of Appeal substituted a sixteen-year minimum term.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 against a life sentence minimum term.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; minimum term quashed and replaced with sixteen years' custody, credited with time already served.
enrichment.ratio: Where aggravating features justify a twenty-year starting point for a pre-2003 murder, a discount of about four years for guilty plea and youth may be appropriate but a fourteen-year term can still be unduly lenient for gratuitous sexually motivated violence.
legal_issues: Appropriate starting point under transitional mandatory life sentence practice
Weight to be given to youth and late guilty plea
Whether fourteen years adequately reflected sexual motivation and extreme violence
Effect of removal of double jeopardy consideration in minimum term references

confidence.notes: Short reference judgment with agreed starting point and explicit substituted term.

notes: Football club administration asset sale; contingent transfer fees excluded as outstanding debts.

enrichment.short_title: Crystal Palace: contingent transfer fees retained by company in administration
key_facts: Crystal Palace FC 1986 Ltd was in administration and sold club assets to CP 2000 Ltd in May 2000 to keep the club in the Football League.
Performance-related transfer fees of £761,732 later accrued from player transfer contracts entered before completion.
The Football League held the fees pending resolution of whether CP 1986 or CP 2000 was entitled to them.
The judge held the fees were excluded from the sold assets as 'other debts outstanding' under clause 2.2(ix); the Court of Appeal dismissed CP 2000's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a High Court decision on an application for directions under section 112 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; contingent transfer fees held payable to the liquidator of CP 1986 rather than CP 2000.
enrichment.ratio: In an insolvency-context business sale listing specified assets, rights to contingent transfer fees not included in the list and expressly excluded as outstanding debts remain with the seller; 'other debts outstanding' in clause 2.2(ix) includes contingent debts.
legal_issues: Whether contingent transfer fees were assets sold under clause 2.1
Construction of concluding 'going concern' language in clause 2.1
Whether clause 2.2(ix) excluded contingent fees as outstanding debts
Commercial purpose of administrators retaining near-term receivables for creditors
linked_authorities: Sirius International Insurance Co v FAI General Insurance Ltd [2004] UKHL 54
In re Brightlife Ltd [1987] 1 Ch 200
Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star [1997] AC 749

notes: Dual AG reference on home invasion robbery; two-and-a-half-year terms replaced with four years.

enrichment.short_title: AG References 144/145/2004: home robbery sentences increased to four years
key_facts: McShefferty and Johnston pleaded guilty to robbing Mrs Douglas in her home early on 25 April 2004 by tricking entry, claiming to have a gun, and stealing her car keys and purse.
They used her car in a second robbery the same morning; Johnston was eighteen, on bail, and had a substantial record including prior robbery.
Miss Recorder Gargan sentenced each to thirty months' concurrent on the home robbery, with Johnston also serving fifteen months on other offences.
The Attorney General referred the home robbery sentences as unduly lenient and the Court of Appeal substituted four-year terms, allowing double jeopardy mitigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's references under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 against concurrent thirty-month robbery sentences.
enrichment.outcome: References allowed; thirty-month terms quashed and replaced with four years' imprisonment for McShefferty and four years' detention in a young offender institution for Johnston, concurrent with Johnston's other sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Robbery of a vulnerable elderly victim in her own home while pretending to have a gun, especially by an offender on bail with relevant antecedents, ordinarily merits about five years before reference double jeopardy, making two-and-a-half years unduly lenient.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentencing range for domestic robbery with weapon claim
Aggravation from victim vulnerability, bail status and value of stolen car
Mitigation from early guilty plea and youth
Application of double jeopardy reduction on Attorney General references
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 48 of 2000 [2001] 1 Cr App R(S) 423
Attorney General's Reference No 1 of 1999 [1999] 2 Cr App R(S) 398

notes: Protected disclosure detriment appeal; two-day window held to lack deliberate failure to act.

enrichment.short_title: Pinnington v Swansea: no whistleblowing detriment where dismissal imminent
key_facts: Mrs Pinnington, a school nurse at Ysgol Crug Glas, alleged a non-resuscitation policy and clashed with the headteacher from 1996; she was suspended in July 1998 and dismissed for capability on 3 July 1999.
She claimed detriment under section 47B because protected disclosure provisions took effect on 2 July 1999 while suspension continued.
The employment tribunal rejected unfair dismissal and held any detriment on 2-3 July 1999 was de minimis or caused by ill-health rather than protected disclosures.
The EAT remitted the whistleblowing claim, but the Court of Appeal restored the tribunal decision for lack of any deliberate failure to act after the Act came into force.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal with permission against an Employment Appeal Tribunal order remitting a protected disclosure detriment claim for rehearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal rejection of the section 47B claim restored and remittal set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Section 47B requires detriment by an act or deliberate failure to act after the whistleblowing provisions came into force; where an employer had already decided to dismiss a long-sick suspended employee, failure to lift suspension on the day the Act commenced is not a deliberate failure to act capable of founding detriment.
legal_issues: Whether detriment must occur after 2 July 1999 even if disclosures pre-dated the Act
Whether continuing suspension without review amounted to deliberate failure to act
Whether stigma of suspension for two days could constitute detriment
Whether the tribunal needed to analyse section 43H qualifying disclosure criteria
linked_authorities: Scally v Southern Health and Social Services Board [1992] 1 AC 294
University of Nottingham v Eyett [1999] Pensions LR 17

confidence.notes: Narrow statutory point clearly resolved with allowance of employer appeal.

notes: Pensions Ombudsman appeal on enhanced early retirement agreement; 1987 tax regime construction upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Nortel: pension enhancement agreement construed under 1987 IR regime
key_facts: Mr Lewis, a senior STC executive, negotiated a November 1989 agreement for enhanced early retirement at age 58 using either a salary uplift or capital injection to reach an 'Inland Revenue maximum pension'.

He was made redundant in April 1991 and received a £46,255 lump sum into the pension scheme, but later complained he should have benefited from the more favourable 1989 Inland Revenue early-retirement regime.
The Pensions Ombudsman held the phrase referred to the 1987 regime and dismissed maladministration claims; Lewis appealed on a point of law.
Lawrence Collins J dismissed the appeal, finding the agreement and redundancy settlement barred the claim and no Scally duty to inform Lewis of the 1989 regime arose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law under section 151(4) of the Pension Schemes Act 1993 against a Pensions Ombudsman determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 'Inland Revenue maximum pension' in the 1989 Agreement held to mean the 1987 regime maximum and full-and-final redundancy settlement held to bar the complaint.
enrichment.ratio: An ambiguous pension enhancement promise made before scheme rule changes must be construed against the background that the employee had no statutory or scheme right to the 1989 regime at the time; a senior executive negotiating a dismissal compromise is not within the Scally category for implied advice duties.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'Inland Revenue maximum pension' in the 1989 Agreement
Whether prior October 1989 letter could be used in construction
Whether employer owed a duty to inform Lewis of election to the 1989 regime
Whether March 1991 full-and-final settlement barred the pensions complaint
